1.pericope_label: This Melchisedec, king of Salem, priest of the most high God
debates: Who Melchizedek was: Gill canvasses and rejects the identifications with an angel, the Holy Ghost and the Son of God, on the ground that he is said to be made like unto the Son of God and Christ to be of his order, and rejects Shem because a descent is recorded in Scripture; Henry reports the same two chief opinions, the rabbinic one for Shem and the Christian one for Christ appearing in the flesh, and answers the first from the change of name and the absence of any settlement in Canaan; Ellicott treats the Shem identification as a legend of the later Targums, absent from the oldest, and suspects the whole tradition of speculation has invested the chapter with a mystery not belonging to it

Whether the tithe here binds anyone now: Gill denies it, the act being voluntary, done once and not yearly, and taken from an enemy’s spoils rather than his own substance, and Clarke denies it too, holding that neither this act nor the like custom of other nations has anything to do with tithes as prescribed under Moses or claimed under Christianity, while Barnes infers the contrary, that devoting a tenth to God was recognised as a duty before the Levitical law existed

Where Salem was: Clarke reports that it is generally understood to be Jerusalem though some take it for Shechem, while Ellicott says Jewish tradition affirms strongly that it occupied the site of Jerusalem
outliers: Henry's judgment that God has thought fit to leave us in the dark about Melchizedek precisely so that he might be the livelier type of one whose generation none can declare, and his warning that men who will not be satisfied with what is revealed must rove about in endless conjectures
Ellicott's observation that of the facts recorded in Genesis none is passed over except the gift of bread and wine, the blessing also being mentioned only in general terms

Calvin's account of how remarkable the figure is, that when the whole world had fallen into impiety and Abraham's own father and grandfather had degenerated into idolatry, one king still both retained true religion and performed the office of a priest himself

Chrysostom's account of the rhetorical strategy, that the writer shoots from afar and prepares beforehand, rebuking his readers as weak and then soothing them before entering on the difference of the dispensations, since a man depressed in spirits would not be a ready hearer
Clarke's rabbinic gloss on the name as the justifier of those who dwell in him, which he says is true enough of Christ but false of the city to which the rabbins applied it
Robertson's remark that it is a daring thing to put Melchizedek above Aaron, and his note that the participle for meeting is here transferred to Melchizedek from the king of Sodom

3.pericope_label: Without father, without mother, without descent, abideth a priest continually
debates: What the threefold negation denies: Gill refers it to the priesthood rather than the person, or else to the scriptural record only, since as a mere man he doubtless had parents; Barnes and Ellicott make it the absence of a genealogical table, Ellicott adding that he is introduced suddenly as priest without the only claim familiar to Hebrew readers; Calvin holds that the silence of the Spirit about his birth and death is tantamount to ascribing eternity to him; and Robertson, while agreeing the argument is from silence, adds that it is not to be pressed, that the likeness lies in the picture drawn in Genesis and not in the man, and that such interpretation does not amount to proof

How the priests can be said to take tithes: Ellicott states the objection that the tithe was paid to the Levites and only a tenth of it reached the priests, and answers it twice, that the question is one of position rather than emolument and that the Levites themselves paid tithes to the priests, who thus alone received tithes and paid none; Clarke gives the same tenth-of-the-tenth explanation; Calvin declines it, saying there is no reason to confine so general a declaration that way

What stock Melchizedek came of: Clarke says outright that he was a Canaanite and makes that the point of the argument, since a priest of the most high God belonging to neither Abraham’s line nor Aaron’s answers the objection that the Messiah must come of a priestly stock, while Gill leaves the question among several open possibilities and Calvin refuses to look beyond what Scripture contains
outliers: Gill's report that the Arabic writers supply the parents Scripture omits, one of them making Peleg the father of Melchizedek, and that the Syriac renders the clause that his father and mother are not written in the genealogies
Ellicott's account of the strictness of Jewish priestly pedigrees, which had to give the name not of the father only but of every mother, to ascend to Aaron, and to contain no doubtful link
Wesley's christological distinction, that the Son of God is really without father as to his human nature and without mother as to his divine, and in this also without pedigree

Robertson's cool verdict that the argument from silence, of which the Alexandrian had made much, is not to be pressed, and that such artificial interpretation does not amount to proof but serves only as a parallel or illustration

The shared observation of Ellicott and Robertson on the perfect tenses, which present what is recorded not as belonging to the past but as standing now before us in the unchanging and ever-present word
Wesley's note that where the singular promise is used of Christ, the plural used here takes in other blessings besides

7.pericope_label: The less is blessed of the better; Levi payed tithes in Abraham
debates: In what sense Melchizedek lives: Calvin takes the silence about his death as evidence of life, rests it wholly on his being a type, and rejects as childish the notion that the man who met Abraham is still alive; Barnes attacks the opposite evasion, that only a changing priesthood is contrasted with an unchanging one, arguing that it would never have occurred to anyone but for the difficulty and does not escape it either; Clarke and Ellicott take the middle course that he is represented as living because Scripture records neither death nor successor, Ellicott adding that what he holds he holds by personal right rather than by birth

In what sense Levi paid tithes: Gill and Clarke take it of seminal inclusion, Gill drawing the parallel of all mankind sinning in the loins of Adam, while Barnes expressly denies that Levi actually paid, that Abraham was his appointed representative, or that the act was imputed to him, offering instead the analogy of a father selling an estate to which the son would be heir, and Robertson calls the whole a rabbinical imaginative refinement appealing to Jews

Whether the argument makes trouble for Christ: Calvin raises the objection himself, that Judah of whose seed Christ came paid tithes in Abraham on the same reckoning, and answers that Christ is not simply one of Abraham’s sons but exempted by a peculiar privilege, and that a type is not to be set against its reality since what is subordinate is not in opposition; Ellicott finds no real difficulty once it is granted that pre-eminence depended on descent alone
outliers: Barnes's limitation of the terms, that the less means one of inferior rank and the better one of superior office, neither implying anything about purity or holiness of character, since that is not the point in hand

Clarke's citation of Macknight that the blessing meant is not the simple wishing of good, which inferiors may do to superiors, but the action of one authorised to declare God's intention to bestow good things

Calvin's appeal to the command in Numbers that the priest bless the people, with a promise immediately attached, from which he concludes that the blessing of the priest was not so much man's blessing as God's
Ellicott's observation that the conclusion of the argument, that Melchizedek appears in this act as Abraham's superior, did not seem to the writer necessary to express
Clarke's list of the classical authors in whom the softening idiom is common, and Barnes's report of the judgment that it amounts to an indirect apology for an unusual or unexpected assertion
Robertson's continued cooling of the argument, here calling it a rabbinical imaginative refinement that would appeal to Jewish readers
themes: the less blessed by the greater
dying men and one who liveth
Levi in the loins of Abraham

11.pericope_label: Perfection not by the Levitical priesthood; the priesthood changed, the law changed
debates: How far the change of law reaches: Calvin restricts it to what peculiarly belonged to Moses, the part subordinate to the ancient priesthood, and insists that the rule of life and the gratuitous covenant of life were not abolished; Barnes restricts it on other grounds, that it cannot touch the ten commandments, which were given before the priesthood existed, nor any other part of the moral law, but only the code regulating the priests and their rites; Gill goes furthest, that the priesthood was not translated but utterly abolished, everlasting being limited as such words often are

What the argument from the order of Melchizedek proves: Chrysostom takes the very circumstance that naturally excluded Christ from the priesthood, that he was not after the order of Aaron, and makes it the establishment of his priesthood and the exclusion of the others, since a later type argues the earlier imperfect; Barnes leaves the defect unspecified here and refers it to the sequel; Robertson reduces the point to grammar, a second-class condition and an abstract noun of act rather than state

What the rising of our Lord out of Judah means: Ellicott notes that everywhere else in the New Testament the verb is used of the sun or the light, but that it also denotes the springing up of plants and stands near the Messianic prophecy of the Branch, which he judges much more suitable here, while Robertson takes the commoner sense of rising like the sun
outliers: Calvin's general principle that no covenant between God and man is in force and ratified except it rests on a priesthood, from which he concludes that the law was instituted for the sake of confirming the priesthood and falls with it

Clarke's full definition of perfection as the accomplishment of all for which a priesthood is established, an acceptable service, instruction, pardon, a purged conscience, a soul prepared for heaven, none of which the Levitical law could confer

Clarke's argument, against most interpreters, that the phrase means on account of the priesthood rather than under it, since the law was in fact given before Aaron and his sons were separated to the office
Barnes's careful limitation that the changed law cannot mean the ten commandments, which were given before the institution of the priesthood and did not depend on it
Ellicott's rendering of the other priest as a priest of a different kind rather than one more of the same, and his reading of the question as equivalent to a strong denial
Clarke's observation that whatever difficulties the genealogies present now, none were apprehended in that day, or the enemies of the gospel would have urged them as a chief and unanswerable argument
themes: change of priesthood and change of law
our Lord sprang out of Judah

15.pericope_label: A priest after the power of an endless life; the weak commandment disannulled
debates: How far carnal is a term of reproach: Clarke enters the caution that it does not mean sinful or corrupt but feeble and frail, what may be said of man in his present dying condition; Calvin enters a caution of his own, that the old priesthood was not so carnal but that it was still spiritual, the contrast here concerning only the difference between Christ and Aaron; Barnes and Robertson press the plain sense, that the law was external and that the Levitical priests became priests merely by birth

Whether the Hebrew for ever must mean eternity: Calvin states the Jewish objection at length, that Moses applies the same word to ordinances which have plainly ceased, and answers that when used of the ancient sacrifices it reaches no further than the coming of Christ, under whom the world was renovated, while when used of Christ no end to his age can be found

What the introduction of a better hope introduces: Clarke takes the Greek as a superintroduction set in opposition to the preceding commandment, coming after to do what the law could not do, while Calvin peculiarly makes the Law itself the introduction, a preparation like the elements taught to children, and his editor notes that most translators and commentators read it otherwise
outliers: Barnes's guard on the opening clause, that what is more evident is not our Lord's descent from Judah but the point being established, and that the order proves it more strongly than the tribe
Calvin's marking of the shift of ground, that the argument ran before on the person of the priest and now runs on the nature of the priesthood and the reason it was appointed
Clarke's observation that Melchizedek held the offices of priest and king together, which no Levitical priest ever did, though priest, king and prophet all meet in our Lord
Ellicott's inference that because Christ lives, in virtue of what he is, he is priest, an essential right set against a mere enactment
Robertson's insistence on the exact adjective, fleshen rather than fleshlike, and his note that the term for disannulling is common in the papyri in the legal sense of making void
Clarke's reading of the drawing near as a priestly phrase, the high priest alone approaching once a year and not without blood, where now all believers enter by that blood
themes: the power of an endless life

20.pericope_label: Not without an oath; Jesus the surety of a better covenant
debates: Whose surety Christ is: Barnes takes the word from common life and then expressly rejects the reading of Crellius that Christ is surety for God that he will maintain the covenant, since no such security of the divine faithfulness is needed or possible, holding instead that the suretyship runs on the part of man, that the law shall be honoured and its penalty not fall; Robertson leaves open what Barnes closes, saying it is not clear whether Jesus is God’s pledge to man or man’s to God, and answering that he is in fact both, as Mediator

Whether the word means covenant or testament: Ellicott argues at length for covenant, tracing the Greek term through its Hebrew original, its classical usage, and the old Latin rendering which fixed testament in English, and holding that covenant is the true meaning everywhere in the New Testament with at most one exception; Wesley grants that the word bears both senses; Gill takes both at once, a testament as bequeathing an inheritance confirmed by the testator’s death and a covenant as a compact made with Christ representing the elect

How far the for ever of the oath extends: Clarke limits it to as long as time shall run, until the mediatorial kingdom is superseded by the fixed state of eternity and God is all in all, while Calvin draws the oath toward the excellence of the covenant rather than the duration of the priest, since a priest is made in order that he may be surety of a covenant
outliers: Ellicott's observation that these three verses form a single sentence, the third answering to the first and the middle one parenthetical, and that the remarkable opening of the psalm so often quoted had until now been passed over
Ellicott's note that the word used is very uncommon and denotes the swearing of an oath rather than the oath itself
Clarke's adoption, in place of his own comment, of a long note of Macknight's collecting the occasions on which God interposed an oath, to Abraham, to the rebellious Israelites, to Moses and to David
The inference drawn from those instances, that the Levitical priesthood, being established without an oath, was thereby declared changeable at God's pleasure

Gill's historical detail that no oath attended the installation of Aaron and his sons, and his report of the later oath sworn by the high priest on the day of atonement after the Sadducees arose, which he sets aside as concerning the execution of the office rather than the investiture
Barnes's care to add that Christ's suretyship is no pledge that men shall be saved without holiness, repentance and faith

23.pericope_label: Many priests hindered by death; one who ever liveth to intercede
debates: What the adjective in verse twenty-four means: Barnes prefers the marginal rendering, that the priesthood does not pass from one to another, and denies that the idea is strictly unchangeableness; Ellicott takes it as inviolable and doubts whether the Greek will bear the marginal meaning at all, since none can trespass on a right founded in an indissoluble life; Robertson sides with Ellicott, glossing the word valid or inviolate, while Wesley keeps the marginal sense and Clarke takes it both ways

Whether to the uttermost is temporal or complete: Robertson reports that the Vulgate takes it temporally but that the common meaning is completely or utterly; Calvin’s own version follows the Vulgate and reads for ever, while his editor argues that the original refers not to time but to what is fully done and cites Erasmus, Beza, Capellus and Schleusner; Barnes takes the completeness side, and Clarke will have both senses at once

Whether the phrase attaches to able or to save: Calvin’s editor notes that most join it to save, but argues that since the subject in hand is the perfection of Christ as a priest rather than the character of the salvation, it must be joined to able, giving the sense that he is fully able to save those who come to God through him
outliers: Gill's numbers, that the Jews reckon eighteen high priests under the first temple and more than three hundred under the second, which he reads as proof of the imperfection of that priesthood

Calvin's distinction between this comparison and the earlier one, that before he concluded the ancient priesthood must end because its holders were mortal, whereas here he shows only that Christ remains perpetually a priest
Barnes's limitation, made by no one else, that the reasoning is not designed to prove the priesthood literally eternal, since the necessity for it may cease when all the redeemed are in heaven

Gill's answer to the obvious objection that Christ did die, that death did not forbid him to continue as it does other men, that he died voluntarily and continued but a small time under its power, and that his death was itself a branch of his priestly office
Barnes's admission that the precise mode in which the intercession is made in heaven is not revealed
Clarke's list of six distinct senses the verb for intercession can carry, and Robertson's borrowing of Moffatt's phrase that this intercession has red blood in it, unlike the conception of Philo

26.pericope_label: Such an high priest became us; the Son perfected for evermore
debates: What separate from sinners means: Ellicott sets out both constructions, that joined to what precedes it marks the perfect sinlessness of one who lived among sinners without needing external separation, and that joined to what follows it marks the severance that now exists for the exalted Lord, and he judges the first more probable; Robertson takes the second, referring the participle to the exaltation, and Wesley takes both at once, separated as well as free from sin, and so he was when he left the world

What the daily offering of the high priests refers to: Ellicott alone treats it as a crux, since the language naturally suits the annual day of atonement and neither the morning and evening sacrifices nor the high priest’s daily meat-offering answer to it, and he offers two solutions, either day by day in the sense of each recurrence of that day or the word attached to Jesus alone, which the Greek order would suggest; Wesley glosses it as every yearly day of expiation, while Barnes and Clarke take it of an actual daily sacrifice on the high priest’s behalf

Whether Christ was perfected before being appointed priest: Ellicott enters the caution, made by no one else here, that we are not to understand Jesus as first perfected and then appointed, since it was as high priest that he offered the sacrifice of himself, while Barnes reads the same participle simply as marking an appointment complete and permanent
outliers: Wesley's statement of the whole verse as a paradox, that such a high priest suited us, unholy, mischievous, defiled sinners
Clarke's list of the five qualifications required of the Jewish high priest, each matched to its Hebrew, and his antithesis that Christ was holy and we unholy, harmless and we harmful

Calvin's reading of Aaron's costly vestments as symbols of a holiness far exceeding human virtues, introduced precisely because the reality did not exist, and his note that Christ is not called separate because he repels us from his society

Ellicott's supply of the ritual behind the language, that seven days before the day of atonement the high priest left his house and lodged in the temple, with five washings and ten purifications required of him on the day itself
Clarke's report that the Jews held a priest who neglected his own expiatory sacrifice would be smitten with death, and his quotation of the confession made over that offering
Clarke's dating of the oath nearly five hundred years after the giving of the law, from which he concludes that it abrogates the law
